Jehovah’s Witnesses Imprisoned for Their Faith—By Location
Imprisoned for Their Faith ijwif
Text and formatting changed
Version archived25 July 2026, 17:12 UTC → Change detected13 August 2026, 01:17 UTC 10.3% of text differs
Changed passage
Previous wording
  • Jin-seong Lee has been imprisoned in South Korea since June 2025
Current wording
  • Marina Chaplykina has been imprisoned in Russia since December 2023
Changed passage
Previous wording
  • Over 276 of Jehovah’s Witnesses worldwide are imprisoned for their faith as of May 2026.
Current wording
  • Over 279 of Jehovah’s Witnesses worldwide are imprisoned for their faith as of July 2026.
Changed passage
Previous wording
  • This aggressive opposition has extended into Crimea, where numerous raids and arrests have led to the current imprisonment of 15 of Jehovah’s Witnesses, all charged with promoting extremist activities.
Current wording
  • This aggressive opposition has extended into Crimea, where numerous raids and arrests have led to the current imprisonment of 12 of Jehovah’s Witnesses, all charged with promoting extremist activities.
Changed passage
Previous wording
  • Currently, at least 163 of Jehovah’s Witnesses are either being held in pretrial detention, serving sentences of forced labor, or serving prison terms.
Current wording
  • Currently, at least 159 of Jehovah’s Witnesses are either being held in pretrial detention, serving sentences of forced labor, or serving prison terms.
Changed passage
Previous wording
  • Currently, nine young Jehovah’s Witnesses are imprisoned for conscientiously objecting to military service, with five serving second sentences.
Current wording
  • Currently, ten young Jehovah’s Witnesses are imprisoned for conscientiously objecting to military service, with five serving second sentences.
Removed
Previous wording
  • South Korea
Removed
Previous wording
  • On October 26, 2020, South Korea introduced alternative civilian service (ACS) for conscientious objectors.
  • However, it has been criticized as punitive due to its 36-month duration, twice that of active military service.
  • Despite court challenges, the Constitutional Court of South Korea upheld the system in 2024.
  • Most of Jehovah’s Witnesses have opted to perform ACS despite its harsh conditions.
  • However, thus far, 15 young brothers have objected to this current ACS arrangement.
  • Of those, one is in prison and several are facing trial and potential imprisonment.
Removed
Previous wording
  • Click here
Removed
Previous wording
  • to download a list of Jehovah’s Witnesses currently imprisoned for their faith in South Korea.
Changed passage
Previous wording
  • Currently, 11 Witnesses are imprisoned and 13 are in pretrial detention.
Current wording
  • Currently, 12 Witnesses are imprisoned and 22 are in pretrial detention.

The 1981 edition removes a conciliatory passage present in 1968: 'It is a good thing to show proper respect for the government and appreciation for the beneficial services that it performs. We all have good reason to be glad that the governments under which we live provide roads for travel, schools...'. Rated notable rather than significant because part of the surrounding difference is study-question apparatus that the extractor does not fully strip, so the exact boundaries of the removal should be confirmed against the printed page before this is relied on.

The strongest finding in the backfill so far, and independently corroborated. The 1968 edition supported its 'last days' argument by quoting the book "Famine-1975!", including its forecast that "By 1975 civil disorder, anarchy, military dictatorships, runaway inflation, transportation breakdowns and chaotic unrest will be the order of the day". The 1981 edition removes that quotation entirely and substitutes undated reporting from the London Times of 3 June 1980 about malnutrition; a separate paragraph citing earthquake death tolls as a mark of the 'last days' is deleted outright. The claim being argued is unchanged - only the evidence that had since failed is withdrawn, with nothing telling the reader the earlier edition said otherwise. Corroborated independently against a secondary source that cites the quotation at pp.88-89 of the 1968 printing and confirms its replacement by the 1980 London Times material.

Contains the second documented removal from this book: the 1968 edition quoted US Secretary of State Dean Acheson warning that "in fifteen years from today, this world is going to be too dangerous to live in" - a dated forecast made in 1960, and therefore expired by 1975. The 1981 edition deletes it. The same chapter gains new material describing post-Armageddon conditions ('There will be no more war... Hatred, selfishness, crime and violence will all be things of the past'), so expectation language is not reduced overall - a specific falsifiable forecast is simply replaced with an undated one. Corroborated independently. Note this entry was rated only 'notable' by the automated triage until the rule was extended to treat the outright removal of a time-bound prediction as its own signal; it names no anchor year, so nothing else flagged it.

Doctrinal / policy implicationsReviewed by a person

The 1965 edition restates scripture quotations in New World Translation phrasing where 1954 used older renderings ('shall inherit the earth' becomes 'the righteous ones themselves will possess the earth'). This is a real and systematic editorial change worth recording, but it reflects a change of Bible translation used, not a change in what is taught, so it should not be read as a doctrinal revision.

Substantive doctrinal expansion between the 1953 and 1957 editions rather than rewording. The entry is rewritten so that the Memorial emblems are explained as symbolising Jesus' own body and blood establishing the new covenant 'and to be the basis for the forgiveness of sins for his congregation of 144,000' - tying the emblems explicitly to the 144,000 limit, which the earlier text does not do in this passage. A subsection heading asserting that Christ needs no priestly representative as mediator is also removed. Worth reading alongside the later development of the 'other sheep' partaking question.

Between 1946 and 1952 this chapter is materially restructured, not merely reworded: a passage describing Christ as 'the brightness of God's glory, the express image of His person... seated on the right hand of the Majesty on high' is dropped, and new material is inserted arguing from Solomon sitting 'on the throne of Jehovah as king instead of David his father' that Jesus does not rule from an earthly throne. The subject matter (the nature and manner of Christ's return) is central to this publication. Rated notable rather than significant because the chapter is diffed as a single large unit and some of the difference is paragraph realignment; the specific insertions above were read directly and are real.

Doctrinal / policy implicationsReviewed by a person

Genuine doctrinal expansion between 1946 and 1952 rather than rewording. The 1952 edition inserts material stating that God 'will have on earth righteous, faithful representatives, men of perfect hearts', that blessings will 'be dispensed to the human race. Not from among sin-laden worldly rulers alive today will these be selected', and that such ones 'need never die again but may attain to human perfection' (citing Hebrews 11:10,35). This develops the teaching about the earthly representatives or 'princes' of the new earth. Rated notable rather than significant because the chapter is diffed as one large unit and the boundaries of the insertion should be confirmed against the printed page.

  • The Scriptures written before our common era were written practically all in Hebrew, a portion in Syriac; and in those Scriptures the alphabetic letters for God's name occur, namely, Jod He Vau He (ninb or YHWH), from the first book to the last.
  • This name, symbolized by these four Hebrew consonants, occurs, all together, 6,823 times* in the Hebrew Scriptures.
  • The Hebrew Scriptures were first translated into Greek about 285-247 B.C.; but some time before that the Hebrews began to leave off pronouncing the name, out of a superstitious fear of taking it in vain.
  • Hence whenever they read and came to the name, they pronounced instead the word Adonai (Lord) or Elohim (God).
  • Hence in making that first translation into Greek known as the Septuagint Version (LXX) the translators followed the Hebrew custom and translated the above substitutes for God's name into their Greek version. * Page 39 IT 2 of The Biblical Text in the Making, by Robt.
